#### Discussion

The results of this study indicate that participants were unable to actively discount the brand name information when they were cognitively impaired. We thus obtain evi dence for the use of sound symbolism being effortless such that even when cognitively impaired, the effects filter through to judgments. The results of this study provide cor roborative support to the prior study’s findings that the in ferences of attribute information from brand names and the subsequent evaluations of the brand are automatic processes.

#### GENERAL DISCUSSION

In this article, we provide support for the proposition that consumers gather and process information from brand names in an automatic manner. However, consumers can control for this provided they process information that dis credits the brand name at the time the name is encountered. An important aspect of sound symbolism established in this article is how it affects consumers’ attitudes at the attribute level (hypothesis 1). Consumers may knowingly control for the process when they have access to information that credits or discredits the brand name at the time at which they en counter the brand name (hypothesis 2). Yet, consumers are not fully aware of this process and cannot fully control for the effect; we show evidence for the uncontrollability of the effect unless the name is discredited at the time of encoding (hypothesis 3) and the consumer is not cognitively impaired

(hypothesis 4). These results provide evidence for the au tomatic processing of brand names and their phonetic effects. Our purpose in this article was to understand the process underlying sound symbolism. The basic phenomenon of sound symbolism has been demonstrated for a wide range of sounds across multiple dimensions (Klink 2000). In our article, we focused on the internal validity of our studies in order to build theory about the sound symbolism process. We therefore tested one set of brand names and used a between-subjects test of sound symbolism. This strengthens the existing case for sound symbolism since participants are not aware that sounds are being manipulated or that one brand name should provide different information than an other. Further, we increase the internal validity of the ex periments by testing for phonetic effects when the brand name is not the only information provided to the subject. Additionally, we show that this effect carries through at tribute perceptions to the overall evaluation of the brand. Demonstrating these effects of sound symbolism increases our confidence in the robustness of our theory. Automatic processes in social cognition domains have been demonstrated empirically in various contexts (see Bargh 1989). This article adds to this literature by dem onstrating the automatic use of sound symbolism. This is an important issue to examine, given that if phonetic effects manifest even partially automatically, then this automatic effect will exert a more consistent influence over attitudes and behavior over time (see Bargh 2002). Since sound sym bolism is a fairly common naming device (Begley 2002), it is possible that phonetic links are highly accessible. Atti tudes relating to the phonetic aspects of the brand name would be automatically activated. Considering the limited capacity consumers usually devote to product evaluation (Hoyer 1984), the results of studies 1 and 2 indicate that

under this diminished cognitive capacity, the phonetic ef fects of brand names may be activated and influence choice. If brand name phonetic cues are chronically accessible, con gruency of brand name and product would be of even greater importance. Our studies tested names in which only one phoneme was manipulated. In most categories, where multisyllabic words are the norm, sound symbolism may occur in different po sitions and/or on multiple positions in the same word. This flexibility would not only increase the complexity of the message conveyed by sound symbolism but also may in crease the strength of the effect. This article has focused primarily on the sound symbolism provided by the vowels of a brand name. The role consonants play in brand names and their effects on product evaluations is an underresear ched area. Past research has shown that brand names that begin with hard consonants (i.e., Kodak and Pepsi), elicit higher recognition (Vanden Bergh et al. 1984), and occur more frequently than we would expect from the English lexicon (Schloss 1981). Although linguistic anthropologists have noted phonetic patterns for consonants (i.e., harder sounding consonants tend to represent harder, sharper ob jects than softer sounding consonants), these findings have not been directly tested on brand names. A systematic study of consonants and their interaction with multiple vowels is an avenue worthy of future research. Our studies demonstrated that sound symbolism, although evaluated on the attribute level, affects overall evaluations. We demonstrated that sound symbolism affected the attrib utes of creaminess, sweetness, and richness: three category specific attributes. It appears that consumers will take the broader dimensions that sound symbolism operates upon (e.g., smallness, lightness, mildness, fastness, etc.) and ex trapolate these findings to the specific properties of ice cream. Creating a successful brand name depends not only upon the creation of a name that is congruent with the prod uct category, but one that phonetically fits the positioning of the brand within that product category. Future research could examine whether it is possible to phonetically ma nipulate meaning over a wide range of attributes in a broad set of product categories. The automatic nature of the sound symbolism leads to important implications of this research upon the use of per sonal names as brand names. For example, if the ice cream was named for its maker, Joseph Frish, then the brand name should be seen as less diagnostic, and the phonetic effect should not appear. This assumes that the information as to the name’s origin is known at the time of encoding and that processing capabilities are not constrained. Telling the con sumer that the ice cream was named for the maker after the ice cream has been tasted should have little effect upon consumers’ use of sound symbolism in accordance with our findings. An interesting further study would be where we manipulate the diagnosticity of the name through the use of a personal name versus a purely fictitious name. Over 2,000 years ago, Plato supported the onomatopoetic theory of language by arguing that words were formed by the imitation of ideas in sounds (Jowett 1953). The argument still holds. Sound symbolism shows that the sounds of words still convey meaning. More important, consumers recognize this phonetic meaning and will use it as a source of product information. The effects of time, the influence of foreign languages, the desire of euphony, and elements of chance all distill and, at times, distort the effects of sound sym bolism. Yet even with these caveats, attending to phonetic meanings and leveraging the attribute associations when cre ating a brand image is sound advice when creating a new brand name. ## Summary
Across the provided sources, peer‑reviewed work shows that specific speech sounds in brand names systematically shape consumer judgments (sound symbolism) and that successful brand names exhibit non‑random phonetic patterns. Academic conceptual work offers a framework mapping phonetic cues to meaning along evaluation, potency, and activity. Practitioner sources propose actionable naming criteria (e.g., fluency/pronounceability, distinctiveness) and process steps, and discuss the trade‑offs among descriptive, suggestive, and arbitrary/fanciful names, including implications for trademark protectability. The sources here provide little to no primary empirical evidence on tagline recall or on financial market effects of corporate name changes; note these as open questions.

## Key Findings
- Sound symbolism shifts product attribute judgments and preferences [6]
  - Lab studies show that brand names constructed with different vowel types (e.g., front vs. back vowels) lead consumers to infer different product attributes (e.g., smaller/lighter vs. larger/heavier) in line with established phonetic symbolism; these phonetic manipulations also influence consumer judgments and choices [6]. The article reports statistically significant effects but does not provide a simple single “effect size” summary in the abstract; use it directionally to align sounds with desired attribute inferences [6].

- Phonetic patterns are non‑random among top brand names [1]
  - A large‑scale analysis of leading brand names documents systematic phonetic patterns, consistent with sound symbolism affecting what “sounds good” in market‑successful names [1]. The paper argues that these sounds can “convey product information” and “enhance memory,” but specific quantitative over‑/under‑representation rates by phoneme class must be taken from the paper’s tables; the abstract itself does not list headline percentages [1].

- A semantic‑differential framework (Evaluation–Potency–Activity) to map phonetics to brand meaning [3]
  - This conceptual framework integrates prior findings by classifying sound symbolism along the three canonical semantic‑differential dimensions: evaluation (good–bad), potency (strong–weak), and activity (active–passive). It proposes linking specific phonetic elements to these dimensions to guide name design and interpretation [3]. It is a synthesis, not new empirical evidence.

- A practitioner framework for “what makes a good name”: four linguistic dimensions [2]
  - The vendor framework specifies four measurable dimensions—cognitive fluency (ease of processing/recall), phonetic impact, sound symbolism (fit of phonemes to desired connotations), and distinctiveness (standing apart from competitors). It offers guidance for scoring/rating candidates on these dimensions but provides no peer‑reviewed effect sizes [2].

- Naming process: staged generation, screening (including legal), and testing [5]
  - An academic/industry report on the naming process describes a structured approach: define objectives and criteria; generate many candidates; perform linguistic and legal screening; conduct consumer testing; and make a final selection [5]. The report focuses on process description; any quantitative benchmarks (e.g., typical timelines, number of candidates) must be taken from the report text; the abstracted page here does not list such figures [5].

- Descriptive vs. suggestive vs. arbitrary/fanciful: strategic and trademark trade‑offs (practitioner guidance) [4]
  - A naming expert outlines common categories and their trade‑offs: descriptive names offer immediate meaning but can be harder to protect; suggestive names hint at benefits and are often registrable; arbitrary/fanciful are most distinctive and protectable but require more marketing support to create meaning in consumers’ minds. This is expert opinion without peer‑reviewed quantification [4].

- Cross‑linguistic considerations in sound symbolism [8]
  - Academic work cited on the page indicates that sound symbolism effects can operate across languages and examines implications for global naming (e.g., Lowrey, International Journal of Research in Marketing, 2012; Kronrod, ACR proceedings, 2014). The page signals cross‑linguistic evidence exists but does not summarize effect sizes here [8].

- Illustrative case use of sound symbolism (vendor anecdote) [7]
  - The “Swiffer” example is presented to show how a coined name can suggest speed/motion and sweeping through its sound pattern; this is a practitioner narrative, not experimental evidence [7].

- Memorability and pronounceability
  - Peer‑reviewed sources here link phonetic patterns to processing and memory in general terms [1], and vendor sources emphasize cognitive fluency/pronounceability as naming criteria [2]. The provided academic articles do not report simple numeric effects on recall probabilities in the abstracts supplied here [1][2].

- Trademark availability/registrability
  - The sources provide process guidance (legal screening) and practitioner views on which categories are easier/harder to protect [4][5]. They do not offer empirical registrability rates or quantitative legal risk models [4][5].

- Taglines and recall, and firm value after name changes
  - None of the provided sources supply peer‑reviewed empirical studies quantifying tagline recall or estimating stock/firm value impacts from renaming; these remain open questions within this source set.

## Evidence Quality
- Peer‑reviewed empirical research:
  - Yorkston & Menon (Journal of Consumer Research, 2004) provide controlled experiments showing that phonetic features of names systematically shape product judgments and choices; robust internal validity for sound‑symbolic effects on perception/choice, but the abstract here does not present unified effect sizes [6].
  - Pogacar et al. (published by Springer, 2014) analyze phonetic patterns among top brand names and argue for non‑random, meaningful sound structures with implications for memory and meaning; quantitative detail is in the paper, with conceptual claims evident in the abstract [1].
- Academic conceptual/synthesis:
  - The Oxford repository framework paper proposes EPA mapping for brand name phonetics; useful for theory and design guidance but not new experiments [3].
- Academic/industry report:
  - Kohli & LaBahn (ISBM report) describe real‑world naming processes and steps, giving practical structure but not peer‑reviewed causal evidence on effectiveness [5].
- Practitioner/agency/vendor content:
  - Vibelo blog (framework and heuristics) [2], naming expert video (categorization and trademark trade‑offs) [4], and Identity Bureau post (case anecdote) [7] provide actionable guidance but are not peer‑reviewed and offer no effect sizes.
- Cross‑linguistic scholarship pointer:
  - The Academia.edu page [8] points to peer‑reviewed work (e.g., IJRM 2012) suggesting cross‑language effects, but the page as provided does not present detailed quantitative findings; consult the underlying papers for metrics.

Areas of consensus across sources here:
- Sounds in names can carry meaning that shapes consumer perceptions [1][3][6].
- Aligning phonetics with desired brand attributes and ensuring fluency/distinctiveness are common practitioner recommendations [2][4][5][7].

Areas not quantified or contested in these sources:
- Magnitude of effects on recall, preference, and sales is not summarized in standardized effect sizes in the materials provided.
- Trademark registrability and legal risk are treated qualitatively, not with empirical rates.
- No direct evidence here on whether renaming changes firm value; no tagline recall experiments in this set.

Widely repeated statistics with no traceable primary source here:
- Within these sources, there are no headline statistics such as “plosive consonants increase recall by X%,” “shorter names perform Y% better,” “name changes raise market cap by Z%,” or “taglines improve ad recall by W%.” If such figures circulate elsewhere, they are not documented in the provided materials.

## Concrete Steps (derived from the sources)
- Define positioning and desired connotations
  - Translate positioning into evaluation, potency, and activity targets (e.g., bold/strong/energetic vs. refined/gentle/calm) using the EPA framework as a linguistic brief [3].
- Generate many candidates across name types
  - Explore descriptive, suggestive, and arbitrary/fanciful territories intentionally, understanding the trade‑offs in meaning immediacy vs. protectability and marketing burden [4][5].
- Engineer phonetics to fit desired meanings
  - Use sound symbolism findings to bias toward phonemes that cue target attributes (e.g., vowel quality and consonant classes aligned with perceived size, speed, softness/hardness) and avoid cues that conflict with positioning [1][6].
- Screen for cognitive fluency and distinctiveness
  - Rate candidates on pronounceability, ease of processing, and their distinctiveness relative to competitive names; use structured criteria such as the four linguistic dimensions (fluency, phonetic impact, sound symbolism fit, distinctiveness) [2]. 
- Test with consumers for perceptual fit
  - Adapt experimental tasks from the phonetic symbolism literature (e.g., attribute inference tasks, choice tasks) to validate that names reliably evoke intended associations before commitment [6].
- Conduct linguistic and legal diligence
  - Perform multilingual checks (where relevant) because sound‑symbolic associations can vary across languages, and conduct trademark clearance early; incorporate legal screening as a formal stage in the process [5][8][4].
- Iterate and decide
  - Use combined evidence—qualitative fit (EPA), consumer testing signals (from [6]-style tasks), and practical constraints (distinctiveness, legal clearance)—to converge on a short list and final choice [5][2][4].
